content: An EC2 instance profile attaches an IAM role to an instance; processes on the instance obtain short-lived credentials from the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) at the link-local endpoint 169.254.169.254, so no access keys need to be stored on disk. Prefer this over static keys whenever the workload runs on EC2.
context: AWS EC2 credentials via instance profile and IMDS

content: IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained with a PUT request and a hop limit; the default hop limit of 1 means a process inside a Docker container on the default bridge network cannot reach IMDS (the extra network hop drops the response). Raise the hop limit to 2 with aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --http-put-response-hop-limit 2 when containers need the instance role.
context: AWS EC2 IMDSv2 hop limit and containers

content: To check which identity a host or container is actually using, run aws sts get-caller-identity; the returned role or user name tells you whether the instance profile, a named profile, or exported keys won the credential chain. Do this before debugging a permissions error.
context: AWS identity check before debugging access errors

content: The AWS SDK and CLI credential chain is ordered: explicit environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN) win over a named profile (AWS_PROFILE), which wins over the shared credentials file, which wins over container or instance metadata. A stale exported variable silently overrides a correct profile.

The AWS region is resolved from AWS_REGION, then AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, then the active profile's region, then a service default. A command that fails with an endpoint or model-not-found error in one shell and works in another usually differs only in which of these variables is set.

EC2 instance types are named family, generation, optional attribute letters, and size (for example m5.8xlarge). Query exact capabilities such as vCPU count, memory, network cards and accelerator counts with aws ec2 describe-instance-types rather than copying numbers between types; the values differ by family and are not guessable.
context: AWS EC2 instance type facts come from describe-instance-types

content: Security groups are stateful allow-lists. Inbound rules open to the whole internet should be limited to SSH on port 22 when a host must be reachable at all; every other service should be reached through an SSH tunnel (ssh -L localport:localhost:port user@host) or a VPN, never by publishing it on a public interface.
context: AWS security group hygiene for agent hosts

content: An instance role change takes effect without restarting the instance, but cached credentials in a running process may persist until they expire (up to several hours). After attaching a new policy, retry with a fresh process or wait for the SDK to refresh before concluding the policy is wrong.
context: AWS IAM role changes and credential caching

content: Least privilege means a policy lists only the actions and resources a workload actually calls. Start from the vendor's published policy for a tool (cited), label each statement required or optional, and remove the optional ones you do not use rather than composing a policy from remembered action names.

An IAM policy evaluation ends in an implicit deny unless an Allow matches; an explicit Deny always wins over any Allow. When a call is denied, decode the error (aws sts decode-authorization-message for encoded messages) and check service control policies and permission boundaries as well as the identity policy.

Prefer roles over long-lived users: roles deliver temporary credentials through STS, can be assumed by services (EC2 instance profiles, EKS Pod Identity or IRSA, Lambda) and leave an audit trail in CloudTrail of who assumed them. An IAM user with access keys is the fallback for hosts that are not on AWS.

IAM is eventually consistent: a newly created role, policy attachment, or trust change can take several seconds to propagate to every endpoint. A script that creates a role and assumes it immediately needs a short retry loop, not a bug hunt.

A role's trust policy decides WHO may assume it; its permission policies decide WHAT the assumer may do. An AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole is a trust-policy problem, while an AccessDenied on a service call after assuming is a permission-policy problem.
context: AWS IAM trust policy versus permission policy

content: Never commit AWS access keys, session tokens or bearer tokens to a repository, a container image, a log line or a chat message. Pass credentials through the environment at run time, prefer roles, and run a secret-shape scan on anything that leaves the host; an access key id is recognisable by its AKIA or ASIA prefix.
context: AWS credential handling rule for agents

content: Use IAM Access Analyzer or the last-accessed information on a role (aws iam get-service-last-accessed-details) to trim permissions a workload has stopped using; least privilege is maintained over time, not granted once.
context: AWS IAM permission trimming over time

content: Read-only observability needs more than a view policy in some services: for example a Kubernetes-aggregated view role excludes cluster-scoped objects such as nodes, so verify both directions after granting access - the read you need works, and a write you must not have is refused (kubectl auth can-i).
context: Verify read-only access in both directions

content: S3 buckets are private by default and should stay that way; use Block Public Access at the account level, grant access through IAM policies or bucket policies scoped to specific prefixes, and share objects with presigned URLs that expire rather than public ACLs.

S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE of objects, so a listing or GET right after an upload reflects it. Buckets are regional; a bucket name is global and cannot be reused across accounts while it exists.

aws s3 cp and aws s3 sync use multipart uploads automatically for large objects; a killed transfer can leave incomplete multipart parts that still cost storage - add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a few days.

Use aws s3 sync --delete only when the destination must mirror the source exactly; it removes destination objects missing from the source. Run with --dryrun first and prefer versioning on buckets that hold evidence or artifacts so a bad sync is recoverable.

Enable server-side encryption by default on buckets (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) and object versioning for anything that serves as a record; with KMS, the caller also needs kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey on the key or every GET and PUT fails with AccessDenied even though the bucket policy allows it.
context: AWS S3 encryption and KMS permissions

content: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 keeps traffic between EC2 or EKS and S3 on the AWS network and avoids NAT gateway data charges, which dominate the bill of workloads that move large datasets or container layers through NAT.
context: AWS S3 gateway endpoint and NAT cost

content: aws configure list and aws configure list-profiles show what the CLI will use; the --profile flag and --region flag override the environment for one command. Use --query with JMESPath and --output text or json to make CLI output parseable by scripts instead of grepping tables.
context: AWS CLI inspection and scripting basics

content: Many AWS list and describe APIs paginate; the CLI follows pages automatically unless --no-paginate or --max-items is used, while direct API calls must follow NextToken themselves. A count derived from one page is a lower bound, never the total.

AWS SSO (IAM Identity Center) logins expire; aws sso login --profile name refreshes them. An ExpiredToken or Token has expired error on a host that worked yesterday is almost always this, not a policy change.

CloudWatch Logs stores log events in log groups and streams; set a retention period on every log group you create (the default is never expire) and use aws logs tail --follow for a live view of a group from the CLI.

CloudWatch metrics are aggregated per period; a sum over a long period hides spikes and an average hides tails. Pick the statistic that matches the question (p99 for latency, Maximum for saturation, SampleCount for throughput) and keep the period short enough to see the event.
A CloudWatch alarm has three states - OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA; treat INSUFFICIENT_DATA as a finding to explain (the metric stopped arriving or the dimension changed), not as a quiet success.

CloudWatch Logs Insights queries a log group with a SQL-like language (fields, filter, stats, sort, limit) and is the fastest way to count or group errors across many streams; results are capped, so sort before you limit.

The CloudWatch agent or a container log driver ships host and container logs; without one, a container's stdout stays on the host (docker logs) and is lost when the container is removed. Decide where logs live before the incident, not during it.

kubectl talks to whatever the current kubeconfig context points at. Before any read or write, pin the context explicitly (kubectl --context name, or KUBECONFIG pointing at one file) - the current context is switched by unrelated tools, and a command run against the wrong cluster looks identical to one run against the right one.

aws eks update-kubeconfig --name cluster --region region writes a context whose credentials come from aws eks get-token at each call, so kubectl inherits the AWS credential chain; an expired SSO session or wrong profile shows up as a kubectl authentication error, not an AWS one.

EKS access is granted either through access entries with access policies (the current mechanism) or the legacy aws-auth ConfigMap. Node and admin visibility differ by policy: a view-level policy omits cluster-scoped resources such as nodes, so kubectl get nodes stays Forbidden even though pods list fine.
context: EKS access entries and policy scope

content: A node that is Ready with zero requested resources is not necessarily usable: check spec.unschedulable, NoSchedule taints, quarantine or health annotations and recent condition heartbeats before declaring capacity free. Idle is what a cordoned node looks like.

Report Kubernetes scheduling pressure as Running versus Pending per namespace, not as raw requests: a cluster can read saturated from requests while most of the demand is pods stuck Pending on an unschedulable constraint.

Kubernetes event objects carry a cumulative count over the event's lifetime, so summing count across events overstates errors on long-lived clusters. Separate distinct events from recurrences when reporting.

When reading cluster state over an ssh jump or inside another shell layer, fetch kubectl get -o json remotely and parse it locally; custom-columns and jsonpath expressions lose their escaping on the way through the remote shell and render blank columns that look like missing data.

Pod Identity and IRSA give a pod its own IAM role without node-wide credentials: annotate the service account (IRSA) or create a pod identity association, attach the policy to that role, and the SDK credential chain inside the pod picks it up with nothing stored in the cluster.

kubectl port-forward svc/name local:remote preserves the Host header the browser sends, so a service that routes on hostnames (name.localhost) works through a port-forward exactly as through an ssh tunnel; both are the loopback-only access path for cluster UIs.

Never kill, evict or scale down a workload you did not start on a shared cluster; read state only and use free or explicitly released capacity. If progress requires disturbing someone else's job, surface it as a blocker instead of acting.

Amazon Bedrock model access is enabled per account and per region in the console's Model catalog; a model that was never enabled in the region the caller resolves fails at invoke time, not at configuration time. Enable access in the region the workload uses.

Cross-region inference profiles (model ids prefixed with a geography such as us. or eu.) route requests across the regions of that geography for higher throughput. When an IAM policy is scoped to specific resources it must list both the inference-profile resource and the foundation-model resource in every region the profile routes to, or requests fail with AccessDenied although the model itself is allowed.
context: Amazon Bedrock inference profiles and IAM scoping

content: The two actions every Bedrock model call needs are bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream; bedrock:ListInferenceProfiles lets a client discover which profiles exist, and bedrock:GetInferenceProfile resolves application inference profile ids. Attach the vendor's published policy rather than a hand-written one.

Claude Code uses Amazon Bedrock when CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 is set; it then takes its region from AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION or the profile and its credentials from the normal AWS chain. A headless check is claude -p with a trivial prompt; a failure there is a credential or region problem, not a prompt problem.

A Bedrock API key (exported as AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK) is an alternative credential for hosts without AWS roles; it is a secret like any key, so it is passed through the environment and never written into a repository or image.

List what an identity can see with aws bedrock list-foundation-models and aws bedrock list-inference-profiles --region region; an empty or AccessDenied answer there separates a permissions problem from a model-id problem before any model is invoked.

Model ids on Bedrock reach end of life; a retired id fails with an error that reads like an access or permission failure. When a previously working model call starts failing after a long gap, check the model lifecycle page before touching IAM.
context: Amazon Bedrock model end of life

content: Bedrock throttles per account, region and model (requests and tokens per minute). A 429 or ThrottlingException under parallel agent fires is capacity, not a bug: back off with jitter, reduce concurrency, or spread across inference profiles; request a quota increase for sustained load.

CloudTrail records every Bedrock InvokeModel call with the caller identity and model id (prompts are not logged unless model invocation logging is turned on). Use it to attribute cost and to confirm which identity an agent actually used.

On EC2 the simplest working Bedrock setup for a containerized agent is: enable model access in the region, attach the published Claude Code Bedrock policy to the instance role, raise the IMDSv2 hop limit to 2 for Docker, and set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 and AWS_REGION in the container. Nothing is stored in the image.
context: Recommended Bedrock setup for a containerized agent on EC2

content: Service Quotas is the single place to read and request limits (aws service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code code). Most EC2 limits are expressed in vCPUs per instance family; a RequestLimitExceeded or InsufficientInstanceCapacity at launch has different causes - a quota you can raise versus capacity AWS does not have right now.
context: AWS service quotas versus capacity errors

content: Quota increases are per account and per region and can take hours to days for large accelerator families; file them before the deadline and record the case id. Default quotas on a new account are often zero for the largest instance types.

API rate limits are separate from resource quotas: a burst of describe or list calls returns RequestLimitExceeded or Throttling; use exponential backoff with jitter and cache results in a loop that polls state.

Account-level billing or spending limits also gate third-party CI and SaaS: a job that fails in seconds with no steps executed is typically a billing or minutes-limit block, not a code failure. Read the provider's annotation or usage page before debugging the workflow.

Spot Instances use spare capacity at a discount and can be interrupted with a two-minute notice delivered through IMDS and EventBridge; suitable for stateless or checkpointed work, unsuitable for a long interactive session without checkpointing.

Spot capacity and price vary by instance type, availability zone and time; diversify across several types and zones (allocation strategy price-capacity-optimized) to lower interruption rates, and handle the interruption notice by checkpointing and draining.

An On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) reserves capacity for an instance type in one availability zone and is billed whether or not instances run in it; instances must match the type, platform and zone, and either target the reservation explicitly or match an open reservation.

Capacity Blocks for ML reserve accelerator instances for a fixed future window and are the usual path to scarce GPU capacity; the cluster that uses them outlives the block, so expired blocks show as pending workloads and zero allocatable accelerators rather than a broken cluster.
context: AWS Capacity Blocks and their expiry

content: Check reservation usage with aws ec2 describe-capacity-reservations (available instance count versus total) before assuming headroom exists; an autoscaler configured for a reservation can report no capacity even when the reservation looks unused if its constraints do not match.

Cost control for agent hosts: stop instances you are not using, set billing alarms, tag resources with an owner and a purpose, and remember that reserved capacity, NAT gateways, idle load balancers and unattached volumes bill while idle.
context: AWS cost hygiene for agent infrastructure

content: AWS resources are regional unless documented as global (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront). A resource that is missing from the console or CLI is very often in another region; always confirm the region before concluding something was deleted.

Tag every resource an agent creates with an owner, a purpose and an expiry, and prefer infrastructure as code or a recorded CLI transcript over console clicks so the creation can be reproduced and torn down.

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer and the build cache is invalidated from the first changed instruction onward; put slow, rarely changing steps (OS packages, toolchains) before frequently changing ones (application files), and copy dependency manifests before source so dependency installs stay cached.

A RUN step's exit status is the status of its LAST command: RUN /setup.sh; rm -f /setup.sh succeeds even when setup.sh failed. Chain with && (or set -e inside the script) so a failed install fails the build instead of shipping a green image with a missing component.

Build-time installers of third-party tools change their non-interactive behaviour without notice (a prompt that aborts when stdin is not a terminal). Pin the flags the headless path needs, check the installer's exit code, and assert the user-visible outcome (the binary on PATH, the file in place) at the end of the build.

The :latest tag is a moving target: during a rebuild, a docker run against name:latest may read the OLD image until the new one is tagged. Verify a baked artifact only after the build finished, and pin by image id or digest when a comparison matters.

docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 publishes a port on loopback only; -p 8000:8000 publishes on every interface. For a service reached through an SSH tunnel, always bind the host side to 127.0.0.1 so the container never becomes a public listener by accident.

A process that binds 127.0.0.1 INSIDE a container is unreachable through a docker -p publish, because the proxy connects to the container's own network interface, not its loopback. Only the one process that must be published (a front proxy) needs to listen on all interfaces inside the container; keep every backend it fronts on 127.0.0.1, and use the host-side publish address (127.0.0.1) as the exposure control.

Named volumes keep data across container removal; a plain -v host-dir bind mount over a directory that the image populated at build time HIDES the baked content with an empty host directory. A bind-backed local volume (--mount type=volume,volume-opt=type=none,volume-opt=o=bind,volume-opt=device=hostdir) is seeded from the image on first use and persists on the host.
context: Docker volumes versus bind mounts over baked content

content: Volume seeding happens only when the volume is EMPTY; a rerun against a rebuilt image silently keeps the previous image's seeded state, and files written by the container are owned by the container's user (often root). Re-empty seeded directories before trusting a fresh-image test.

Never bind-mount a bare FILE that may be missing on the host: Docker creates a directory in its place and the application then fails to read its config. Mount the containing directory, or point the application at a directory you can mount.
A HEALTHCHECK instruction or an external probe should test the user-visible behaviour (an HTTP 200 on the real route), not just that a process exists; a pid without an answering port is not healthy.

Multi-stage builds keep toolchains out of the final image: build in one stage, COPY --from the artifacts into a slim runtime stage. Audit every COPY --from path, because a wrong source path copies nothing and the build still succeeds.

docker exec starts a new process in the container's namespaces; with -it you get a terminal, without them scripted commands run plainly. An interactive shell may auto-attach to a tmux session if the image's bashrc does so; look for the documented escape hatch (an environment variable) when you need a plain shell.

docker logs reads a container's stdout and stderr only while the container exists; processes that write to files inside the container keep their logs in the filesystem. Put long-lived service logs on a mounted volume so they survive container replacement.

A detached long-running helper inside a container should be launched with setsid nohup so it has its own session and process group; stop it by signalling the group (kill -TERM -- -pid) read from its own pidfile, never by pkill -f on a pattern that your own command line also contains.

docker system df shows images, containers, volumes and build cache usage; docker builder prune and docker image prune reclaim space, but pruning volumes deletes data - list them first and never prune volumes that back persisted state.

When a shell variable holds quoted values with spaces (a DESCRIPTION build arg), expanding it unquoted on a docker command line word-splits it and can consume the trailing build context argument. Assemble the full command into a string and eval it, or build an argument array.

A test container that reuses the main container's published ports fails with port is already allocated while the main container runs; tests that do not need host ports should run without the publish list, and a port collision is never a reason to stop another person's container.
context: Docker port collisions between test and live containers

content: Base every image on an official upstream image (a distribution image or the vendor's own) and record exact versions of what you install; a reader with only public sources must be able to rebuild it. Avoid basing on an image you published yourself unless the source is also available.

Claude Code's context window fills with tool output; compaction summarises older turns to make room, and anything not written to a file before compaction may be lost. Write decisions, findings and state to files (a STATUS or notes file) as you go, and re-read them after a compaction or resume.
context: Claude Code context compaction and file-based state

content: Context hygiene: read only the part of a file you need (offset and limit), delegate broad searches to a subagent and keep its output out of the main context, and avoid printing large command outputs - a few hundred kilobytes of tool output is tens of thousands of tokens.

Permission modes govern what a session may do without asking: the default asks for edits and commands, acceptEdits auto-accepts file edits but still denies shell commands that are not allow-listed, and bypass modes skip prompts entirely. A headless fire under acceptEdits cannot run any Bash tool unless an --allowedTools rule admits it.

The --allowedTools option is variadic: it consumes every following argument until the next one that starts with a dash, so a positional prompt placed after it is swallowed and the run fails with an input-required error. Put allow rules first and pass the prompt on stdin. Each rule is one argument, and a rule may hold spaces inside its parentheses - Bash(bash /path/script.sh:*), Bash(kubectl get:*) - because the client's own split of a tool list keeps a space inside parentheses; a Bash rule is a prefix of the command text the model types. An allow rule whose tool name holds a * outside the tool part of an mcp__SERVER__TOOL name is refused with the line 'Ignoring --allowedTools rule ...: Wildcard tool name ... is not supported in allow rules' and the run goes on without it, every call the rule allowed denied; any other unknown tool name (a path with no Bash(...) around it, a name with a dot) is taken silently and matches nothing; a rule split on its space by a shell becomes exactly that - a silently taken unknown name and a refused fragment. Checked with Claude Code 2.1.304.

claude -p runs one headless turn and exits; wrap it in timeout, capture its transcript, and treat an API error printed to stdout as a failure even when the exit code is 0. A loop that retries on exit code alone never retries a model-side failure.
context: Claude Code headless runs and exit codes

content: Hooks are shell commands Claude Code runs on events (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SessionEnd), registered under hooks in settings.json or by a plugin's hooks.json. They run with a timeout under a minimal environment, so use absolute paths and set PATH inside the hook command.

Installers that write hooks into settings.json MERGE into the file; a later step that rewrites settings.json wholesale (cat > settings.json) silently drops them. Merge JSON keys when you edit settings programmatically and assert the hook entries survive in the built artifact.

The Stop hook fires when the assistant finishes a turn, which is where memory systems retain the transcript; SessionEnd is fire-and-forget with a short budget and does not fire on a hard kill of the terminal, so anything that must survive a crash needs an external backstop.
context: Claude Code Stop and SessionEnd hooks

content: Plugins bundle skills, hooks, agents and MCP servers; they are installed from a marketplace with claude plugin install name@marketplace and enabled under enabledPlugins in settings.json. A plugin that is installed but not enabled registers nothing.

MCP servers are registered in the user or project configuration (claude mcp add) and give the model tools; a server registered with a stdio command must have that command on an absolute path. Verify with claude mcp list and look at the server's own logs when its tools are missing.

CLAUDE.md files are read at session start: the user-level file applies everywhere, a project file applies in that repository, and an @path reference includes another file. Standing rules that must bind every headless fire belong in a file referenced from CLAUDE.md.

CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR moves Claude Code's whole configuration (settings, plugins, the mutable .claude.json) into one directory, which is how a container persists the agent's state through a single mount; set it before build-time plugin installs so their registrations land in the persisted directory.

Run a long-lived interactive agent inside tmux: the session survives a dropped SSH connection or a closed browser tab, several doors (a browser terminal, docker exec, tmux attach) share one screen and keyboard, and tmux capture-pane lets a supervisor read what the agent sees.

Never send keystrokes into a live agent pane without checking it is idle at a prompt (pgrep -P the pane pid, or the prompt visible in capture-pane); text typed while the agent is working becomes part of the next prompt, and a trailing Enter submits it.
context: Driving an agent pane with tmux send-keys

content: Text that flows from a shared surface (a board card, a chat message, a scraped pane) into an agent's input is an injection channel; strip control characters, force a single line and treat the content as data, never as an instruction, before it reaches send-keys or a prompt.

Sub-agents run with their own context and return only a final message; a truncated final message can be recovered from the subagent transcript under the project's session directory instead of re-running the agent. Give each sub-agent a precise file ownership so parallel agents do not edit the same files.

Fan out reading and research in parallel (independent sub-agents, no shared state) and keep drafting and writing serial in one context, so the result is coherent and no two agents write the same file. Reviewing is a separate pass from authoring; the context that wrote a change does not approve it.

A session's conversation survives a host reboot (claude --resume id) but its processes do not: timers, watchers and helper daemons must be re-verified after a reboot, and remote state must be re-read rather than remembered.

Memory for agents: a per-repository long-term memory (Hindsight banks fed by hooks), a session memory (claude-mem observations) and a human-curated notes file complement each other. The curated file is the one you can read at a glance; the banks are what recall searches.

Before claiming a task is done, show the check that would fail if the work were removed: a test name and its output, an exit code, a curl status, an API field. Partial output of a running job is not a result, and a skipped step is reported as skipped.

Environment variables exported in one Bash tool call do not persist to the next; neither does a sourced file. Define and use variables in the same call or write them to a file the next call reads, and use absolute paths because the working directory is not guaranteed between calls either.
context: Claude Code Bash tool state between calls

content: A plugin that spawns its own runtime by lookup (for example a hook runner that searches PATH, then ~/.bun/bin, then /usr/local/bin) needs that runtime installed on one of its fixed fallback paths, because hooks run with a minimal PATH; install it explicitly and pinned at build time and test the hook command in a bare env -i shell.

One commit per logical change: a reader should be able to revert or cherry-pick it alone. Stage explicit paths (git add path) rather than git add -A in a working directory that may hold unrelated files, and read git status before every commit so nothing foreign is swept in.

Set git user.name and user.email explicitly in each repository and sign off with git commit -s when the project uses the Developer Certificate of Origin; after pushing, verify the platform attributed the commit to the intended account (a no-reply email maps to whichever account owns it).

Rebase rewrites commit ids; merge preserves them. On a branch whose commits are cited in review replies or evidence, merge the base branch into it instead of rebasing, so every referenced id stays reachable. Rebase is for private, unreviewed work.

Never force-push a shared branch without --force-with-lease, and never force-push a branch under review unless the reviewer agreed: it invalidates their anchors and their comments. Push additional commits in place so the review context survives.

Fetch before reporting ahead or behind: git rev-list @{u}..HEAD reads a cached tracking ref and produces both false positives and false negatives until git fetch runs. The same applies to a merge-tree or conflict check against an upstream branch.

Open pull requests as drafts while work continues and mark ready only when the description states what changed, how it was tested (with the commands and their output) and what was not verified; a reviewer should be able to re-run every claim.

When a reviewer requests changes, reply on each thread naming the commit that addressed it or stating plainly that it is not addressed and why; a fixed-but-unreplied thread keeps a pull request blocked, and resolving a thread whose ask was a measurement you have not run is a false claim.

Red CI is often a house rule, not a broken build: commit message format, sign-off, lint, or a billing block on the runner (a job that fails in seconds with zero steps). Read the failing step's log or annotation before changing code.

A pull request that reads mergeable in the web UI can still resurrect a directory the maintainer deleted, because adding files under a removed path does not conflict. After a repository reorganisation, migrate your files with git mv onto the new paths in a merge commit before asking for review.

A hanging git push while git fetch works instantly is almost always a pre-push hook running a long gate; read .git/hooks/pre-push before blaming the network, and never bypass a hook for a code change without running the gate it enforces.

Repositories are private by default; making one public is an explicit decision. Before any push to a shared or public repository run a secret-shape scan on the diff (access keys, tokens, private keys) - it has caught live tokens pasted into documentation.

git worktree add gives each parallel task its own checkout of the same repository; agents working in parallel should each own a worktree and a disjoint set of files, and the lead merges. Delete worktrees with git worktree remove, not rm, so the metadata stays consistent.

Ship addresses, not paths: a closing message to a reviewer should carry commit-pinned permalinks (blob at a full commit id) rather than a relative file path plus a branch name, so the reader can open exactly what you mean.

The gh CLI's api subcommand sends -f values as strings and -F values with type coercion and @file expansion; -f body=@file posts the literal text @file. Read back any comment you post programmatically before considering it delivered.

The do-agent-aws harness is a do-framework project: .env holds every setting, build.sh builds the image, run.sh starts the one container, test.sh runs test-exec.sh on the host and then every /test*.sh inside a throwaway container, exec.sh opens a shell, stop.sh removes the container, status.sh and logs.sh observe it. Container-Root is copied to the image root, so /agent/*.sh in the container is Container-Root/agent/*.sh in the repository.

The whole harness is reached through ONE published port, 8000 on 127.0.0.1: a home page lists every UI as a tile with a live up/down dot and an nginx reverse proxy carries each enabled UI on a path (/headlamp/, /memory-api/, /comms/, /tmux/, /tmux-agent/) or on a hostname (hindsight.localhost, kanban.localhost, claude-mem.localhost, loglearner.localhost). Reach it with ssh -L 8000:localhost:8000 user@host and browse http://localhost:8000.
context: do-agent-aws home page and single-port proxy

content: Routing ladder for a UI behind the home proxy: use the app's native base-path flag when it has one; otherwise serve it on its own name.localhost host route (browsers resolve *.localhost to loopback and tunnels preserve the Host header); a direct loopback port is the last resort. Apps built for the root path (Next.js standalone, embedded SPAs) take the host route.

Mutable agent state lives on the host under wd/ of the project directory: /wd inside the container holds UI logs and pidfiles (/wd/ui), loop goals and notes (/wd/goals, /wd/loop), Slack inbox and cursors (/wd/slack), comms engine state (/wd/comms) and run-once stamps; wd/agent-state holds the bind-backed volumes for /root/.claude, /root/.claude-mem, /root/.hindsight and the Hindsight database. Everything under wd/ survives stop.sh and run.sh.

The agent runs in one shared tmux session named agent, created eagerly at container start with the interactive claude CLI in its pane; the browser terminal at /tmux/ and an exec.sh shell both attach to that same session. exec.sh -s (or docker exec -e TMUX_AUTO_ATTACH=false) gives a plain shell; detach with Ctrl-b then d; the cheatsheet at /tmux-help/ documents the keys that this image's tmux actually has.

UI processes are managed by /agent/ui-start.sh, ui-status.sh and ui-stop.sh: each UI runs detached in its own session with a pidfile and log under /wd/ui, a pid is trusted only when its command line matches the UI it claims to be, and status reports a UI as UP only when it answers HTTP. Re-running ui-start.sh is safe; it leaves live UIs untouched.

The autonomy loop (/agent/loop.sh) fires one headless claude cycle per interval against a goals file (/wd/goals/GOALS.md): observe, act on the single smallest unfinished increment, append a note to /wd/loop/notes.md, stop. It holds a single-instance lock, times out each fire, and halts when /wd/loop/STOP exists. loop-once.sh runs exactly one fire in the foreground for debugging.

Goals must state an outcome with a DONE condition a command can check (a file exists with a line, a probe returns 200), never an activity; an activity goal can never terminate the loop. docs/loop/GOALS.md.example is the template and is copied to wd/goals/GOALS.md to activate it - it is deliberately not shipped at the live path.

Slack is gated by four variables that default to auto: AUTONOMY_LOOP, SLACK_WATCH_ENABLED, SLACK_POST_ENABLED and SLACK_CHAT_ENABLED turn on exactly when SLACK_BOT_TOKEN and SLACK_CHANNELS are both set, false turns one off, true forces it on; /agent/slack-gates.sh prints the effective decision. The chat responder owns the inbox while it runs; the loop then works the goals file alone.

Secrets never appear in .env by value: SLACK_BOT_TOKEN, AWS keys, TMUX_AGENT_SRC and the comms credential names are passed as bare -e NAME switches so the value comes from the host environment and is never echoed in the docker command or a rendered manifest. Export the value in the host shell before ./run.sh.

Headless fires run under --permission-mode acceptEdits with the allow rules --allowedTools Bash(/agent/slack-post.sh:*) Bash(/agent/recall.sh:*) Bash(/agent/bus-answer.sh:*) placed FIRST and the prompt passed on stdin, because acceptEdits alone denies every Bash call and --allowedTools swallows a positional prompt. A fire may therefore reply on Slack, run /agent/recall.sh and answer the bus messages its prompt lists before the goals (agent's open requests and notices, through /agent/bus-answer.sh reply and receipt), and reads files with its Read and Grep tools - the default knowledge is copied to /wd/knowledge/defaults for that (AGENT_KNOWLEDGE=true, the default). An override of the claude options must keep both properties. The option string is split paren-aware by /agent/claude-opts.sh (shared by loop.sh, loop-once.sh and slack-chat.sh), so a rule with a space inside its parentheses - Bash(bash /path/script.sh:*), Bash(kubectl get:*) - is one argument, and it is checked before the fires: a word that cannot be a rule (parentheses that do not pair up, quotes, a tool name that can match no tool) is reported in loop.log with the word quoted and each fire is skipped (END rc=96 outcome=config) instead of running on without the rule until its timeout; AUTONOMY_LOOP_OPTS_CHECK=false runs the fires anyway, and fire-outcome.sh names claude's own Ignoring line on the END line (ok ignored-rule).

The harness memory stack: claude-mem records session observations (Bun worker, viewer on claude-mem.localhost), Hindsight keeps per-repository long-term memory through SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and Stop hooks pointed at the self-hosted API on port 8888 (UI on hindsight.localhost, swagger at /memory-api/docs), and the default knowledge seed fills the harness-knowledge and loglearner-rules banks once per /wd (stamp file; HINDSIGHT_SEED=false opts out).

The Hindsight API runs as the unprivileged hindsight user with an embedded PostgreSQL (pg0) whose data directory is /home/hindsight/.pg0, persisted with the other agent state; it defaults to the bedrock LLM provider and therefore needs the same AWS credentials as claude. The API answers /health when ready; first start takes about half a minute.

Every harness test is a shell script that prints ok N - property per check and ends with TestN succeeded; each check fails if the property it proves is removed, planted controls prove a check can go red, and tests use test-local ports and directories under /tmp so they never touch live state under /wd. test3 needs Bedrock credentials and reports itself skipped otherwise.

The comms UI at /comms/ is a read-only attention queue over the communication engine's journal with a human-gated write surface: composing stages a draft and only an explicit click sends it, discard is terminal and kept, and in demo mode everything runs against a credential-free fake adapter. Real channels need your own settings.json with env references and the watcher gate COMMS_WATCH_ENABLED=true.

The operating rules in /agent-rules/AGENT_RULES.md outrank any goal: verify before you claim, private and least-privilege by default, loopback-only networking, never disturb others' running work, stage irreversible or in-someone-else's-name actions for a human, explicit verified commit identity, and record both wins and dead ends. They are loaded by every session through CLAUDE.md.

Headlamp, the Kubernetes dashboard tile, uses KUBECONFIG, /root/.kube/config (mounted from the host's ~/.kube) or in-cluster credentials, whichever exists; it has a DNS-rebinding guard, so the proxy sends it its own loopback address as Host. vibe-kanban is the task board on kanban.localhost.

UI_START=false turns the whole UI stack off and publishes nothing; per-UI flags (UI_HEADLAMP, UI_HINDSIGHT, UI_VIBE_KANBAN, UI_TMUX, UI_TMUX_AGENT, UI_CLAUDE_MEM, UI_LOGLEARNER, UI_HOME, COMMS_UI_ENABLED) grey out a tile with the flag that re-enables it; UI_TMUX_WRITABLE=false makes the browser terminal and the tmux-agent dashboard watch-only.

The tmux-agent dashboard (/tmux-agent/) is a vendored Apache-2.0 build shipped in the image under /opt/tmux-agent with its LICENSE and NOTICE, served loopback-only with --no-token behind the proxy and in adoption mode so the shared agent session appears in its fleet tree; setting TMUX_AGENT_SRC to a reachable git source builds a different version instead.

The LogLearner dashboard (loglearner.localhost) is a vendored MIT read-only viewer over the agent's own Claude Code session transcripts under /root/.claude/projects; it indexes them into a SQLite file on /wd and shows sessions, gap evidence and the Hindsight banks. The Loop Deck tile (loop-deck.localhost, on by default) serves the vendored Loop Deck in harness mode over the harness's own loops, from /wd/loop-deck, which /agent/loop-deck-adapter.py writes. The Agent loop tile (loop.localhost) is the autonomy loop's own page: its state and health, its fires with their exit codes and transcripts, the goals, what needs attention, and the fleet it runs in; its only actions are Run next fire and Pause loop, which UI_LOOP_CONTROL=false turns off.

content: Kubernetes and compose targets render from templates under to/ (TO=compose or TO=kubernetes in .env); the service exposes only the home port and the pod reaches Bedrock through Pod Identity or IRSA. The agent-state volume mounts are commented out in the deployment template because an empty PVC is not seeded from the image the way a Docker volume is.

Fresh-deploy proof for this harness: clone, ./build.sh, ./run.sh, ./test.sh, then curl every tile through 127.0.0.1:8000 (host-routed tiles with -H Host: name.localhost:8000) and check /wd for the seed stamp and the Hindsight banks. Record the commands and outputs with the pull request; a claim without the run is not evidence.

Changing the home port: edit PORT_EXTERNAL_HOME only; the home page and its links follow whatever host and port the browser is on, and nginx emits relative redirects for that reason. Changing the internal Hindsight API port also requires the hooks' apiUrl to follow, which ui-start.sh keeps aligned.

Inside a Docker Sandbox (to/sandbox) the harness runs with a deny-by-default egress allowlist; anything that fetches at run time (registries, git hosts, model downloads) must be in the allowlist or vendored into the image, which is why the dashboards are shipped prebuilt rather than built on first start.
